A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same continual-unlearning study. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support comparison despite expanded experiments and conference reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original ConAbl and EraseDiff experiments, regularizer comparisons, semantic-similarity analyses, and retention-loss curvature measurements.

after.justification: v2 reports original ConAbl, SculpMem, and ESD experiments, including celebrity erasure, SDXL evaluation, and additional analyses of unlearning dynamics.

M1.justification: The update-norm penalties, selective fine-tuning rule, TIES merging procedure, and auxiliary-concept gradient projection remain unchanged in Sections 6–7. Evaluating these regularizers with SculpMem and ESD does not introduce a new proposed algorithm component.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates UNLEARNCANVAS style and object erasure. v2 retains this coverage and adds identity-based erasure involving six target celebrities and six held-out celebrities, plus general-generation retention using MS-COCO prompts (Appendix A.2–A.3). This extends evaluation beyond the original concept domains.

E2.justification: SculpMem replaces EraseDiff as the second principal evaluated unlearning method in Section 5 and Appendix A. ESD is newly evaluated for SDXL celebrity erasure. v2 also adds the simultaneous comparator to the ConAbl regularizer comparison in Figure 6, where v1 showed sequential unlearning and its regularized variants.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce the GIPHY celebrity classifier, FID and CLIP Score on 5,000 COCO-prompt images, and SDXL. Appendix B.2 replaces the base-checkpoint perturbation experiment with relative UNet perturbations across base and independently unlearned checkpoints on held-out retention concepts. Appendices D–E add experiments applying 99% UA early stopping to both strategies; these are additional controls, not evidence that all original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Section 8 and Appendices C–E examine anchor-dependent parameter updates, concept-erasure thresholds under model interpolation, drift under matched stopping criteria, and cumulative training costs. Appendix B.2 substantially revises the curvature analysis. These add mechanistic, sensitivity, and optimization-budget investigations absent from v1.

E5.justification: v1's curvature table reports means and standard deviations. v2's Figure 18 instead presents per-model trends, medians, 95% intervals across models, distributions, and Spearman and Mann–Whitney U p-values. This expands statistical reporting for one analysis; neither version establishes repeated training-run uncertainty for the main benchmark comparisons.

E6.justification: EraseDiff results are removed, while SculpMem, celebrity, SDXL, and new diagnostic results are reported. For example, v2 Figure 17 reports harmonic means of 82.6 for model merging, 50.8 for projection, and 87.0 for their combination with ESD/SDXL; these are new-setting results, not improvements over v1 scores. The original ConAbl combination scores in Figure 8 remain 89.6 for styles and 88.3 for objects.

T1.justification: The continual-unlearning definition, projection construction, first-order invariance lemma and proof, and Taylor/Cauchy–Schwarz retention-loss derivation are retained. The revised curvature experiment and interpolation analysis do not change these formal results.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central claims about utility collapse, parameter drift, regularization, and semantic-aware projection. The conclusion now specifically recommends selective fine-tuning plus gradient projection for in-domain and cross-domain retention, refining v1's general statement that the add-ons provide strong baselines.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets anchor-based unlearning as representation replacement, explains how erasure thresholds complicate merging, and argues that excess sequential drift persists beyond optimization-step differences. It also qualifies smoothness as local and identifies unresolved adversarial recovery, architecture, objective, and modality generalization questions. These substantially expand v1's interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix D newly discloses that the original sequential experiments used method-default iteration budgets while simultaneous unlearning used validation checks every 100 iterations and a 99% UA stopping threshold. Appendix B.2 specifies relative UNet perturbations and matched minibatches, diffusion noise, and timesteps. These improve procedural documentation without supplying a comprehensive implementation specification.

R1.justification: v2 introduces SculpMem and COCO references and several additional continual-learning, generation, and safety citations. SculpMem replaces EraseDiff as the prominent recent-method example. The broader novelty positioning and detailed discussions of semantic awareness and model merging remain largely unchanged; the latter move from Appendix C to F.

P1.justification: Most of the abstract, introduction, and Sections 3–7 preserve their wording and ordering. Local revisions affect related work, the conclusion, captions, and organizational summaries; Section 8 and additional appendix sections are inserted. Conference headers, affiliations, acknowledgments, and an LLM-use disclosure are also added, without a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds extensive celebrity/SDXL plots, an anchor-correlation heatmap, interpolation panels, a controlled-drift heatmap, and a training-cost plot. It replaces the curvature table with distribution plots and introduces an optimization-step table. Existing diagrams, legends, captions, and placements are revised, while v1's Figure 9 normalized-gain plot disappears and the document adopts ICLR formatting.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence was confined to style/object erasure on one diffusion architecture and lacked an explicit stopping-budget control for its drift explanation. v2's identity-erasure and SDXL evaluations, controlled drift experiment, and measured training costs substantially strengthen generality and evidential support (Appendices A, D–E). Removing EraseDiff results loses evidence, and celebrity summary-metric captions and cumulative-step terminology remain unclear, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.
